questions.set_intro: Imagine that a friend calls to ask about greenery in the home. You talk by phone about keeping indoor plants.
questions.question: What is the hardest part of caring for indoor plants, and why?
questions.model_answer: The hardest part is giving each plant the right amount of water. Too much rots the roots, and a dark corner makes that mistake worse.

questions.set_intro: Imagine that a friend calls to ask about greenery in the home. You talk by phone about keeping indoor plants.
questions.question: Would you recommend indoor plants to someone who has never grown anything? Why or why not?
questions.model_answer: Yes, I would recommend one easy indoor plant to a complete beginner. A pothos forgives a missed week and does not need strong sun. I would tell the person to buy one plant, not five, and to touch the soil before adding water. One healthy plant is more encouraging than a shelf of brown leaves, and it teaches the basic habit without much risk.

questions.question: Do you think schools should start the day later in the morning? Give reasons for your opinion.
questions.model_answer: I think schools should start the day later in the morning. Many teenagers are still half asleep at seven, so an early class often turns into rereading the same page instead of real learning. A start around eight-thirty would fit their sleep better, and students might arrive more alert and less likely to skip breakfast. Younger children can be different, so a later start matters most in middle school and high school. Schools would need to adjust buses and after-school clubs, and that takes planning. Even so, I would rather move the bell than keep asking tired students to learn when their minds are not ready. Alert students take part more in class discussions, and teachers spend less time repeating themselves.
